extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of natural philosophy (observers/experimentalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for investigating and arguing about natural phenomena: emphasizes empiricism (experience before reason), careful repetition and measurement of experiments, stepwise analysis of phenomena, and how to structure proofs (define terms, use observations as illustrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on experience rather than imaginative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus, you who observe rely not on authors who have merely by their imagination wished to be interpreters between nature and man, but on those alone who have applied their minds not to the hints of nature but to the results of their experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not depend on speculative authority or imagination; prefer investigators who have applied their minds to the results of experience. Be aware that seemingly similar experiments may yield different results (the deceptiveness of experiments). Use empirical results as the primary basis for claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin investigations from experiment then seek the reason
rubrics_metrics.description: This is the true rule by which investigations of natural phenomena must proceed; and although nature herself begins from the reason and ends in the result, we must pursue the contrary course and begin, as I said above, from experience and by it seek out the reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying a phenomenon, first perform and cite experiments/observations, then deduce and demonstrate the causal reason. Structure discourse to present experiment first and then reasoning that explains it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat experiments to confirm results
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deducing a general rule from this case repeat the experiment two or three times and see if the same results are produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always repeat trials multiple times so that accidental occurrences or experimental mishap do not vitiate the conclusion. The experimental example (two balls dropped touching each other) should be repeated several times to avoid deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiments as illustrations supporting propositions (not vice versa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not forget that you must put forward propositions adducing the above-mentioned facts as illustrations, not as propositions,--that would be too simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed facts to illustrate and support tentative propositions; avoid presenting unsupported propositions as settled facts. Ensure propositions are grounded in observed examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite concrete experiments first, then demonstrate by reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Before I proceed further I will make some experiments, because it is my intention to cite the experiment first and then to demonstrate by reasoning how such an experiment must necessarily take effect in such a manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly present experimental setup and results before offering theoretical explanation. This is the declared procedural order for trustworthy investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When collecting facts, state the practical uses under each proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: When you collect facts relating to the science of the motion of water, remember to place under every proposition the uses to which it may be applied, in order that this knowledge may not be fruitless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For every empirical proposition about natural phenomena, record its potential applications and uses so knowledge remains practical and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat experiments with controls to avoid accidental contact or error
rubrics_metrics.description: The experiment to prove the above-mentioned theorem respecting motion must be made thus: Take two balls of equal weight and shape and let them fall from a great height so that when they start falling they touch one another, and let the investigator stand on the ground and watch whether the contact is maintained during their fall. This experiment must be repeated several times, so that the trial may not be marred by any accident and the experiment vitiated and the spectator deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with clear, controllable conditions (equal weight/shape, known initial contact) and observe carefully; repeat to exclude accident and observer deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire knowledge stepwise; master details before proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: if you wish to attain to a thorough knowledge of the forms of objects, you will begin by studying the details, and not proceed to the second until you have committed the first to memory and mastered it in practice, and if you do otherwise you will be wasting your time and protracting your studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn by progressive mastery: study and memorize foundational details, practice them, then move to the next. Emphasizes diligence (speed) and sequential learning rather than skipping steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and quantify phenomena where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how many times the diameter of the sun will go into its course in twenty-four hours. And thus we can see whether Epicurus was correct in saying the sun was only as large as it appeared to be...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative measurements and simple arithmetic to test claims (e.g., angular diameter × distance traveled). Quantification exposes absurdities in speculative assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of apparent sameness of experiments (experiments may be deceptive)
rubrics_metrics.description: And you must realize the deceptiveness of experiments; because those which often appear to be one and the same are often different, as is shown here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume two experiments that look similar are equivalent; check conditions and repeat to detect subtle differences. Vigilance against deceptive appearances is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and define terms and perceptual mechanisms when arguing astronomical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: First of all define the eye; then show how the twinkling of a star exists really in the eye, and why one star should twinkle more than another, and how the rays of the stars are born in the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving astronomical or perceptual claims, begin by defining relevant organs/processes (e.g., the eye), explain perceptual phenomena mechanistically (why twinkling occurs), and connect these to observations to build the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present the explanation of observed effects by relating them to causes (effects correspond to the force of their cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: A spherical body which possesses a dense and resisting superficies will move as much in the rebound resulting from the resistance of a smooth and solid plane as it would if you threw it freely through the air, if the force applied be equal in both cases... if you measure the distance accomplished by the aforesaid bounds you will find that they equal the length of distance through which a similar object set in motion by an equal force would travel freely through the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate measured effects directly to the forces applied; look for conservation-like relations (total effect corresponding to initial impressed force) and verify by measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat empirical observation and analysis of details for vision and perception
rubrics_metrics.description: We know definitely that sight is infinitely swift and in an instant of time perceives countless shapes, nevertheless it only sees one object at a time...you will instantly realize that it is full of various letters, but you will not realize at that moment what these letters are nor what they signify; wherefore you will have to proceed word by word and line by line to take cognizance of these letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break perceptual phenomena into analysable steps; examine how immediate perception yields parts that must be attended to sequentially. Use detailed, incremental analysis for sensory phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume nature is governed by consistent laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature never breaks her laws. Nature is constrained by the cause of her laws which dwells inborn in her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the working hypothesis that natural operations follow consistent, discoverable laws; use this assumption when forming experiments and explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek causes not only effects; understanding causes reduces need for experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Without reason no effect is produced in nature; understand the reason and you will not need experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to discover causal explanations behind observed effects; while experience is primary, causal understanding reduces reliance on repeated observation for every case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record practical analogies and exemplars (e.g., world as man in miniature) to elucidate complex systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancients called man the world in miniature... because man being composed of earth, water, air and fire, the body of the earth resembles the body of man...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete analogies and structural parallels to make complex natural systems intelligible, but ground analogies in observed correspondences rather than mere speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proposing controversial claims (e.g., earth as star) structure a demonstrative discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: In your discourse you must prove that the earth is a star like the moon, and thus you will bear witness to the glory of our universe! And thus you must discourse on the size of many stars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For bold or counter‑intuitive claims, lay out a clear discursive program: define terms, present experiments/observations, explain perceptual mechanisms, and compute/measure where possible to support the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: When developing experimental explanations, include examples and note limitations of analogy (beware misplaced analogies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bird is an instrument which operates by mathematical laws, and man can reproduce all the movements of this instrument, but cannot attain to the intensity of its power; and can only succeed in acquiring balance...such an instrument constructed by man lacks only the soul of the bird...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies (e.g., bird vs man made instrument) to guide design and expectations, but recognize limits (differences in 'soul' or subtle adaptations) and avoid overextending analogical conclusions.
